problems.description: WELCOME_TIMEOUT (5.0) is defined in server.py but never referenced — dead symbol consistent with the measured smells +1.
broadcast() returns self.client_count (count after failed sends are pruned), but its docstring promises the number of clients the message was delivered to — misleading return semantics.

test_server.py contains the two commit-attributable convention violations from the measured 9: test classes not PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE. The other 7 measured violations live in pre-existing files (app.py, test_backbone.py, test_channels.py, test_rate_limit_history.py) not touched by this commit.
No backpressure handling on outbound sends; a slow client can stall broadcast delivery to all other clients (single event loop). Acceptable for session-1 greenfield but worth flagging.

strengths: Clean single-file module with explicit lifecycle (start/stop/handle_connection) and a canonical JSON wire format enforced by make_message() with type validation.
Correct asyncio usage — the documented thread-safety reasoning for the lock-free client registry is sound.
Broad test coverage (231 lines) accompanies the implementation; error paths (invalid JSON, unsupported message, unknown target, client disconnect) are handled explicitly.
Module and method docstrings are thorough; type hints present on public signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, well-tested greenfield WebSocket server with only minor debt (a dead constant, a misleading broadcast return value, and two test-file naming violations), where the measured convention score of 0.81 understates the commit's own quality since 7 of 9 violations come from pre-existing files.

problems.description: Channel extraction logic `data.get("channel") or payload.get("channel")` is duplicated across all three branches (broadcast/subscribe/unsubscribe); refactor to a single helper. Consistent with SonarQube duplications delta +7.8%.
Cognitive complexity +32 in handle_connection from the chained elif dispatch; a message-type dispatch table (dict of handler callables) would keep the growth linear as new types are added.

broadcast() return-value semantics changed from `self.client_count` to `len(targets) - len(failed)` (delivered count). More correct, but existing callers relying on the old semantics should be checked.
Potential dead code: `subscribed_channels()` and the `channel_names` property are defined but never consumed by the handler or any REST endpoint.

Convention score 0.81 per static analysis — PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violations concentrated in test files (test_backbone.py, test_channels.py, test_rate_limit_history.py, test_server.py, app.py); minor but should be normalized for consistency.
_drop_client iterates all channels and subscriber sets on every disconnect; O(channels × subscribers). Fine at this scale but worth noting if channel counts grow.

strengths: Consolidated cleanup: `_drop_client` gives a single path that removes a client from the registry and all channel subscriptions, preserving the previous finally-block behavior.
Reuses existing patterns: make_message/_send helpers, single-event-loop thread-safety reasoning, and the dict-registry idiom from _clients extended consistently to _channels.
Empty channels are pruned on unsubscribe (del when set empties), and channel_subscribers/channels_info return sorted, deterministic output.
Subscribe is idempotent via set semantics, and missing-channel messages return proper error responses instead of raising.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured channel feature that fits the existing NotificationServer architecture and reuses its patterns, but introduces mild technical debt through triplicated channel-extraction logic and rising cognitive complexity in the message dispatcher.

problems.description: Dual source of truth: subscription/connection state exists both in the server's local mirror (_local_channels/_client_channels) and in Redis, written fire-and-forget via _background() with exceptions swallowed, so the two mirrors can silently drift; _hydrate() on restart reloads Redis state over local state, which can resurrect ghost subscribers or drop valid ones after an unclean exit.

Pervasive bare `except Exception: pass/continue` (MessageStore.store, server._record, _deliver_event, startup cleanup, broker.close) makes persistence and Redis failures invisible, contradicting the module docstring's durability guarantee ('persists every distributed message').

Leaky pluggable-backbone abstraction: LocalBroker is implemented by reaching into server internals (_local_channels, _client_channels, _clients, _deliver_event) through the circular `broker.server` back-reference, so the Broker interface is not self-contained and cannot be understood in isolation.
RedisBroker.unregister_client and channel_names call scan_iter over the whole keyspace (O(N)) — unregister runs per disconnect, so this grows with the number of channels.

Mechanical checker reports 0.81 / 9 violations, but inspection shows they flag lowercase 'classes' and module constants in pre-existing test files (test_channels.py, test_server.py, test_rate_limit_history.py) and app.py — which is not part of this worktree's tree — rather than code introduced by this commit; the introduced code follows PascalCase/UPPER_CASE/snake_case conventions correctly.

strengths: Clean pluggable-backbone design: Broker ABC with LocalBroker/RedisBroker implementations, DI through NotificationServer.__init__, and a default_backbone() factory — mirrors the existing TRANSPORT env-var pattern.
Backward compatibility preserved: with REDIS_URL unset the LocalBroker fallback keeps the historical single-instance in-memory behaviour, so the integration is additive rather than breaking.

Comprehensive integration tests with fakeredis covering multi-server pub/sub fanout, cross-server direct messages, restart-state hydration, SQLite persistence, and pagination — exercising the real WebSocket + REST paths.
Strong docstrings documenting the architecture and tradeoffs; UPPER_CASE module constants, type-hinted public signatures, and parameterized SQL throughout broker.py.
Constructive refactor of server.py that keeps existing APIs (make_message, SUPPORTED_TYPES, subscribe/unsubscribe, REST handler style) intact while threading the new backbone through.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-architected integration session that cleanly adds a pluggable Redis/SQLite backbone behind a Broker abstraction with strong fakeredis-backed tests and backward-compatible fallback, held back only by silent error-swallowing and a dual-state drift risk; the 0.81 convention score reflects largely pre-existing or false-positive test-file flags rather than the introduced code.

problems.description: Transports reach into NotificationServer private members (_server, _new_client_id, _drop_client, _rest_handler), so the 'pluggable' layer is coupled to undocumented server internals — a new transport author must know the private API, undercutting the stated extensibility goal.
Connection tracking is split across layers (BaseTransport.connections plus whatever server-side registry remains); if the server also keeps a client registry the two can diverge.
Convention score 0.81 is dragged down by violations in app.py and test files (PascalCase, UPPER_CASE constants) that this commit never touched (+0 files); the commit's own diff is fully compliant.

strengths: Clean extension point: BaseTransport ABC + self-registering @register_transport registry with env-var (TRANSPORT) selection, so new transports slot in without touching core logic.
Behavior preserved: REST endpoints (/health, /channels, /messages), message backbone wiring, and make_message structure all carried over intact — no regression from the +273/-121 refactor.
Idiomatic new code: type hints, ABC/abstractmethod contract, per-method docstrings, and PascalCase classes / snake_case methods consistent with repo conventions.
Maintainability improved: duplication down -0.3%, bugs +0, smells +0, complexity +4 is negligible for a 273-line refactor.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-executed transport-layer refactor with a clean registry pattern and preserved behavior, marred only by transports reaching into server private members — and a convention score that reflects pre-existing violations in untouched test/app files rather than this commit.

problems.description: history() and cleanup() compare timestamps as raw strings in SQLite text columns; correctness depends on every writer storing the exact canonical UTC ISO format (including microsecond presence). _normalize_since() normalizes the input but not the stored rows, so any legacy or foreign writer breaks ordering silently.
RateLimiter.allow() Redis path is INCR-then-EXPIRE, not atomic: a crash between the two calls leaves a counter key that never expires, leaking Redis memory over time.

RateLimiter uses time.time() for the Redis window key but time.monotonic() for the in-process fallback; the inconsistent time bases mean a client migrating between backends (or a server restart) sees a fresh, possibly empty window.
9 convention violations in the newly added test files (and app.py): classes not in PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE — consistent with the measured 0.81 convention score.
Cognitive complexity +55 (measured) is notable for a ~650-line change, driven mostly by the multi-branch history()/cleanup()/RateLimiter logic; acceptable but worth decomposing.

strengths: Extracts a _row_to_dict helper to deduplicate row mapping, reusing existing async aiosqlite patterns
_normalize_since() handles naive timestamps and explicitly reasons through the microsecond string-ordering edge case, showing real correctness awareness
Rate limiter mirrors the existing LocalBroker fallback philosophy — the server keeps working out of the box without Redis
New cross-cutting features (per-client rate limiting, paginated history with has_more, TTL cleanup) fit the notification-service domain and follow the env-var-with-default config pattern
Cleanup and reset paths make the added functionality testable
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting commit (rate limiting, TTL cleanup, paginated history) that respects existing async/config/fallback patterns, with the main debts being fragile string-comparison timestamps in SQLite and a minor Redis counter-leak race, and the sole convention failures confined to test-class naming and constant casing.

compounding_issues: Seed codebase (Flask Todo app.py) is domain-mismatched and never used: Session 1 greenfield-built a WebSocket notification server from scratch, and the dead app.py was carried through all 5 commits unremoved and unreconciled
Repo hygiene: __pycache__/*.pyc binaries were committed in Sessions 1-2 before .gitignore arrived in Session 3, and remain tracked afterward

NotificationServer is a growing monolith (server.py 210 -> 635 lines): the Session 4 transport refactor extracted client I/O but the core class kept absorbing rate limiting, persistence, routing, and lifecycle in one place
Unused dead constant WELCOME_TIMEOUT carried from Session 1 to the end; send_direct persists a message to SQLite before confirming the target exists
Rate limiting applies only to inbound client messages, not outbound fanout, so a single broadcast can still amplify into a self-inflicted delivery storm
key_decisions: Session 1: abandon the seed and greenfield a websockets-based async server with a canonical {type, payload, timestamp} wire format and single-event-loop thread-safety model

Session 3: commit to a Redis pub/sub message backbone (RedisBroker with LocalBroker fallback) plus SQLite MessageStore persistence — the most consequential architecture choice, enabling multi-instance fanout and durable history

Session 4: introduce a pluggable BaseTransport ABC with @register_transport and the TRANSPORT env var, decoupling all client I/O from core notification logic and setting up future transports (SSE/polling/TCP)
Session 5: add Redis-backed per-client rate limiting with an in-process fallback, message TTL retention with a startup cleanup task, and a chronological paginated /history endpoint
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and measurably across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a clean, well-documented greenfield core with a passing test suite; Session 2 added channels as a disciplined additive feature; Session 3 was the boldest step, bolting on Redis pub/sub distribution and SQLite persistence with new backbone tests; Session 4 was a genuinely valuable transport-abstraction refactor (394 lines churned in server.py with no new tests — risky but landed cleanly, all prior tests still green); Session 5 capped the arc with production-grade cross-cutting concerns. Tests accumulated 13 -> 26 -> 31 -> 31 -> 45, all passing at the final commit, and docstring/interface quality held to a consistently high standard throughout. The arc is clearly ascending, with the only persistent wart being the abandoned seed file and committed bytecode artifacts.
story_review.summary: A well-orchestrated, monotonic build-up from greenfield WebSocket core to a distributed, rate-limited, retention-managed notification platform, marred only by the never-reconciled seed app and minor repo hygiene debt.
